system.name: Melange lobbying data and LDA linkage
system.description: LobbyView/LDA ingestion and its analytic uses: finance-client classification, the finance report join, the member-year lobbying network, the circular lobbied-member link, the FEC-to-LDA bridge test, contact inference, the ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster, the contested-bills registry and the industry-axes tensor.

components.name: LDA finance-client classification and report join
components.computes: Bank, credit union or other classification with HIGH/LOW confidence. Joined finance reports: 322,473 issue-coded reports; ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M.
components.method: Name regex with guards. NAICS is linkage metadata only. Fail-closed guards. Vintage 2024-10-25; coverage reliable through 2021.
assumptions: Client names are decisive for finance classification
empirical_questions: How does name-based classification compare with Kim et al. positions-based industry assignment?
components.heading: LDA finance-client classification and report join

components.name: Lobbying member-year network and circular lobbied-member link
components.computes: client x bioguide x year dyads (63,991 member-years). Edges are the sponsor and cosponsors of lobbied bills.
components.method: P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so it is REFUTED as evidence of influence. LD-2 filings never name members.
assumptions: The bill-roster join is not a lobbying-contact measure
empirical_questions: Using an independent contact measure, does lobbying precede cosponsorship more than chance?
components.heading: Lobbying member-year network and circular lobbied-member link

components.name: FEC to LDA bridge test
components.computes: Relation between FEC giving and LDA lobbying network change.
components.method: Round 1 VOID. Round 2 p = .098 (Spearman +0.259, N = 52). Round 3: raw rho +0.153, but the four-control partial is -0.0002. Closed pending a new vintage. FEC as a 42-month leading indicator is a candidate heuristic.
empirical_questions: Does industry FEC giving lead LDA lobbying expenditure after controlling for firm size and sector?
components.heading: FEC to LDA bridge test

components.name: Contact inference (activity to member)
components.computes: Matches lobbying activity descriptions to members.
components.method: Gold positives name the member. Negatives come from the same organisation's roster join, split 50/50 by organisation. Contamination is estimated by a recall sample.
empirical_questions: What is the precision of description-based contact inference against blind labels?
components.heading: Contact inference (activity to member)

components.name: Ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster
components.computes: Predicted cosponsor joins on open bills. A frozen forecast of 265,396 predictions is unscored.
components.method: Ridge logistic regression. Scoring against the lobbied-member table would be circular.
assumptions: Network and lobbying features predict joins
empirical_questions: Does the forecaster beat a cosponsorship-history baseline (Brandenberger reciprocity; Russo et al.)?
components.heading: Ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster

components.name: Contested-bills registry
components.computes: Per-bill mode (standard, advisory or contested) adding a counterparty term (Romero Moreno 2021).
components.method: Loader shipped; engine wiring not built.
assumptions: Owner ratification is the only admission route
empirical_questions: On bills where banks and CUs oppose each other, does relative lobbying spend predict outcome?
components.heading: Contested-bills registry

evidence.title: A hypergraph analysis of the European Commission lobby network
evidence.claim: Each edge comes from an official register entry that names both the EC official and the interest representative in a dated meeting. Duplicate meetings were fuzzy-merged at partial ratio >= 70 (460 pairs).
evidence.system_side: LD-2 filings never name a member, so the bill-roster join gives P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction. It is REFUTED as evidence of influence, and LDA stays an identity source only (D-021).
evidence.transfer: The paper shows what a valid lobbying-contact layer requires: a register that names both parties to the contact. No US congressional equivalent exists, so the design does not carry over to LDA. It is a benchmark for any future contact source, not a method to apply.

evidence.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Firm-politician-year LPMs (Table 3, N=16,428,834, public manufacturing firms NAICS 31-33 x members of Congress, 2008-2017): a first-time donation in year t raises P(firm lobbies a bill the politician sponsored, cosponsored or handled in committee, same year) by 0.102-0.118 (cols 1-4), against a base of about 0.05. The table text sets L = t-1; the matched DiD uses a 3-year no-donation history (L=3). Matched DiD (Fig 5): about +8.5 pp at t for the Senate, falling to about 3 pp (caption: 3.2) at t+3; the House is described as stronger but no number is given. Fig 6: effects larger for corporate PACs and particularly stronger for committee membership; the authors say the effects disappear within two to three years.
evidence.system_side: Bridge round 3 is a LOCKED corroboration look: X = FEC relational exposure, Y = rebuilt LDA attention, per member x industry (credit_union, fintech, crypto) x cycle, 2023-2026; pooled fractional-rank Spearman with member-blocked permutation (5,000) and four controls (party, chamber, volume-within-party, House Financial Services / Senate Banking membership). Recorded result: raw rho +0.1525 (member-blocked p=0.0146), four-control partial -0.0002; UNCORROBORATED, window CLOSED, predictor language barred. The brain's '42-month lead' (lobbyview-collector.md:124; memory lda_bridge.lead_months=42) is a data-freshness gap (FEC data runs about 42 months past LobbyView coverage), not a measured behavioral donation-to-lobbying lag.
evidence.transfer: Estimands differ: Kim identifies within-pair onset timing (pair FE or matched DiD on first-time donations) among public manufacturing firms; the bridge is a between-member cross-section over concurrent windows dominated by financial trade associations. The bridge Y credits only sponsor and cosponsor rosters, so the committee-referral outcome channel that carries Kim's strongest effect is absent; the bridge's committee control is a covariate (Kim also controls for 'powerful committee' membership), so 'controls away Kim's channel' is an interpretation, not a demonstrated fact. Appendix E's trade-association slope (beta 0.8 vs corporations beta 2) is a cube-root, 1999-2000, organization-level replication of Ansolabehere et al., not Kim's dyad design. So the bridge null does not refute Kim and Kim does not license predictor language. Kim does NOT bear on the '42-month lead' as written, because that number is a data-recency gap, not a behavioral lead; at most Kim argues against reading it as one. A successor onset/pair/committee-referral test is a new prereg and Paul's gate.

evidence.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Outcome Y=1 if firm i lobbies any bill in year t related to politician j as sponsor, co-sponsor, or member of the committee the bill is assigned to. For the descriptive Lobby $ column, a firm's annual lobbying spend is divided by the number of unique bills lobbied and the per-bill amount is allocated across all connected politicians (sponsor, co-sponsors, committee members); the authors call this a highly noisy measure and use the binary link in the analysis. Donation onset is the separately measured treatment.
evidence.system_side: The shipped network credits every sponsor and cosponsor of each lobbied bill (build_network_2021_rebuild.py docstring line 13; lobby_interactions.py:4-5 'did this organization lobby a bill this member sponsored or cosponsored'). The brain records the lobbied-member link as circular (P(joined | lobbied)=1 by construction); LD-2 never names members. committee_referrals is parsed (build_network_2021_rebuild.py:5466-5697) but not used to credit members.
evidence.transfer: Kim uses the same roster join only as an outcome against an independently timed treatment (donation onset), the non-circular use. That supports keeping the join as 'whose bills did this org lobby on', never as contact. Kim adds a committee-referral channel the system's join lacks. The paper gives no warrant to read the join as contact. Adopting Kim's dollar allocation would make LDA a weight source (barred by D-021).

evidence.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: The DiD design keys on first-time donations (firm i gives to politician j for the first time in L=3 years). The effect appears in year t and declines (Senate about 8.5 pp to about 3 pp by t+3). Corporate PAC donations show larger effects than CEO or employee donations, though all show ties. Effects are particularly stronger for committee membership.
evidence.system_side: DRAFT spec channel C3 (donation co-occurrence): org-PAC and (with Gate G1) lobbyist money reaching member m near quarter q, as gave-in-quarter, gave-in-cycle and amount tiers; zero = no-evidence; binding bar on donation-predicts/causes wording. C2 = dated committee activity on cited bills as venue relevance. Fused feature budget hard cap 10.
evidence.transfer: Design hints only: an onset feature (first gift to m in 3 years) instead of gave-in-cycle, a short decay horizon, and a C2 x C3 interaction. They must fit the 10-feature cap and the prereg/one-look discipline. Kim's outcome is lobbying a related bill, not contact, so the paper cannot serve as validation (LobbyView-as-validation is barred). Sample transfer is weak: public manufacturing firms vs financial associations and CUs.

evidence.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network
evidence.claim: The LDA does not require registrants to disclose direct contacts with legislators, so the paper infers legislator connections from lobbyists' disclosed past employment; a legislator is included if at least one active lobbyist worked for them. About 90% of lobbyists have no documented government or legislator association, and 20% had a known government connection in 2023.
evidence.system_side: The member-year network credits every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill (build_network_2021_rebuild.py:13), so the system treats the link as REFUTED as evidence of influence. The interaction ledger states that the LD-2 form has no position field and ships position_basis='not_disclosed'.
evidence.transfer: The evidence carries over fully because it describes the same federal LD-2 form. The paper uses the same data and states plainly that legislator contact is unobserved, so nothing in LD-2 can rescue the bill-roster join. An independent contact measure is still required. The paper's own legislator edges come from revolving-door disclosure, so they are not contact evidence either, and influence language is barred on them.

evidence.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network
evidence.claim: For the SOPA case study, only about 40% of the clients lobbying on SOPA in Q4 2011 could be mapped to NAICS sectors through Compustat, and the probabilistic analysis is restricted to them. Client disambiguation is search-assisted and the paper says it is weak for long-bankrupt firms and non-public-facing firms that resolve to third-party directories. The analysis window runs 1999-2023.
evidence.system_side: Client names decide classification and NAICS is only suggestive. High confidence requires a name rule. In the 2024-10-25 bulk-export vintage, issue-code coverage collapses after filing_year 2021.
evidence.transfer: The 40% figure is for one bill-quarter sample (SOPA, Q4 2011), not all LobbyView clients; no all-client or finance-client coverage share is reported. It supports not relying on NAICS for credit-union versus bank classification only as an illustration. Whether the post-2021 issue-code collapse is a bulk-export vintage artifact remains UNVERIFIED and should be checked against the OSF release.

evidence.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network
evidence.claim: The paper defines a government-association function g(l,y), which is monotone in year, and a political-association function p(l,y), which is not monotone. Both are built from one-time disclosures of covered positions, and lobbyists give no timelines for those positions, so recency cannot be established.
evidence.system_side: No shipped code path for the contact-inference lane was found; the nearest shipped surface records position_basis='not_disclosed'. The gold-positive design described for the component is not verifiable from code.
evidence.transfer: The g and p definitions can be reused as documented, timestamp-free association labels. They are not contact evidence and must not become edge weights (D-021). Any use needs a 'no timeline' label, because the paper itself says it cannot date the ties.

evidence.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
evidence.claim: Bombardini and Trebbi (2012) report an average share of lobbying by individual firms of 67% (median 96%); industries with lower concentration and lower product differentiation spend a higher share of lobbying through trade associations. Huneeus and Kim (2019) put business-association lobbying at less than a quarter of all lobbying expenses.
evidence.system_side: Finance clients are classified bank, CU or other from client names. The brain records that directional positions sit with trade associations (CUNA 174 Support / 12 Oppose, NAFCU 168 Support / 23 Oppose; the 22 pinned fintech and crypto firms hold 1 directional position out of 56). ABA lobbying is $228M against CUNA's $93M.
evidence.transfer: The prediction is cross-industry, from Bombardini and Trebbi's 2012 trade-issue sample. The review gives no CU-specific figure.

evidence.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
evidence.claim: Kang (2016) models lobbying as Tullock contests among four energy coalitions, mapped at the level of policy provisions decoupled from bills. Policies with no lobbying are enacted about 1% of the time and those with two or more lobbying players about 24%, which the review says implies substantial selection. The structural effect of lobbying is much smaller (0.021%-0.415%); entry has multiple equilibria resolved by a selection assumption.
evidence.system_side: A per-bill contested or advisory registry with explicit counterparty industries. The loader has shipped. No engine consumer exists, and the CONTESTED_V1 dial is only planned.
evidence.transfer: A contest success function is a candidate form for the planned counterparty term, but Kang's model carries misspecification symptoms and selects among multiple equilibria by assumption. The 1% vs 24% contrast reflects selection and must not be quoted as a lobbying effect. Weighting contests by LDA spend would conflict with D-021.

evidence.title: An Application of Data Mining Techniques to Explore Congressional Lobbying Records for Patterns in Pediatric Special Interest Expenditures Prior to the Affordable Care Act
evidence.claim: The LDA XML amount fields do not separate lobbying expenditures from income, and no identifier lets a researcher split them. Expenses under $5,000 are a checkbox with no amount, and client income over $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000.
evidence.system_side: The LobbyView collector parses is_self_filer per report (line 847) and parses a blank amount as 0.0 (line 844). Its per-side, per-year amount_sum (905) and finance_amount_sum (909), and its top-spender total_amount (932), add every report's amount whether self-filer expense or hired-firm income; self-filer dollars are kept only as a sub-sum (912). The auto-memory note lobbyview-integration-2026-07-31.md (not the brain) records 'ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M' and 'self-filer = expense, hired firm = gross income'. The claim that an in-house expense figure already includes payments to outside firms comes from LDA guidance as cited in commit 914623152, not from this paper.
evidence.transfer: The hazard carries over: the LD-2 amount semantics the paper describes still apply. The paper's claim that the two series cannot be separated does not carry over to LobbyView, which exposes is_self_filer; the collector could split them and does not in these aggregates. The LobbyView window and the 2024-10-25 vintage were not re-checked here. Whether the $228M ABA figure is the mixed total_amount, and how large the overlap is, stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).

evidence.title: An Application of Data Mining Techniques to Explore Congressional Lobbying Records for Patterns in Pediatric Special Interest Expenditures Prior to the Affordable Care Act
evidence.claim: Pediatric items sit in single filings alongside unrelated issues (Medicare Part B vaccine coverage, Medicaid pediatric vaccines, FDA biologics, pandemic preparedness), so dollars spent on pediatric lobbying cannot be isolated. The paper nonetheless reports dollar sums by umbrella code from a Filing x Issue merge: Taxation/Internal Revenue Code $527,147,333 and Health Issues $436,651,121 for Q4 2009, with no filing-count denominator.
evidence.system_side: For finance-joined reports the collector increments a per-code report count (per_code[code] += 1) and does not spread or repeat dollars across codes. The auto-memory receipt '322,473 finance-coded reports' is a report count.
evidence.transfer: Applies to any LDA source where one report carries several issue codes. That the paper's per-code totals count a multi-code filing under each code is an inference from the merge description, not stated by the authors; treat the totals as non-benchmarks either way.

evidence.title: Lobbying coalitions and their determinants: a systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Issue-context hypotheses are supported 6 of 7 (85.7%; 16-article subsample, unstratified by polity). The authors conclude that groups coalesce more in a highly salient and conflictual policy context (condition i). Similar groups are not the only ones to ally: 'strange bedfellows' coalitions form when the policy context makes them strategically useful (Junk 2019; Beyers and De Bruycker 2018). Prior work found that issue characteristics can matter more than organization-level factors.
evidence.system_side: The registry stores an explicit per-bill counterparty set, never a global one (docstring lines 4-10). Standard mode is the default when no registry or record exists. Each record needs a non-empty ratified_by and a ratified_date. No consumer is wired yet: the CONTESTED_V1 dial is described as future.
evidence.transfer: The evidence comes from interest-group studies, mostly US and EU, about whether groups form coalitions, not whether they win. It supports per-bill alignment as a structural choice. It says nothing about how large any counterparty term should be, which stays owner policy.

evidence.title: Lobbying coalitions and their determinants: a systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Relative-weakness hypotheses are supported 11 of 12 (91.7%; Table 4, 16-article subsample, unstratified). The paper says weaker groups 'lobby in packs' to pool resources. A significant minority of studies (Beyers and Donas 2014; Gray and Lowery 1998) finds the opposite, which suggests a minimum resource threshold. The authors leave the question open.
evidence.system_side: INDUSTRY_SIDE makes credit_union the only 'ours' industry. Community banks, fintech, crypto, telecom and credit_arms are all 'opposition'. The registry rejects any ours-side industry in counterparty_industries, so a record can hold only counterparties and has no field for an allied industry.
evidence.transfer: An ally field would be descriptive (who stood with CUs on bill X). LDA may identify allies, but under D-021 co-lobbying cannot become an edge or a weight. The coalition-to-influence link is contradictory (p. 8), so the field should not change any score without its own validation.

evidence.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports
evidence.claim: Bill-level positions show opposing interest groups on the same bill. Coal-deregulation bills (H.R. 3409, 112th; H.R. 806, 115th) are opposed by environmental groups and supported by commercial entities, while an environmental-protection bill (S. 847, 112th) shows the reverse. Subject Oppose ratios: Public lands and natural resources 0.354 (51 bills), Environmental protection 0.280 (108 bills). The paper does not tabulate inter-industry conflict per bill.
evidence.system_side: The contested-bills registry is a loader for per-bill counterparty sets that Paul ratifies. No consumer exists today (CONTESTED_V1 is unopened), and the bundle surfaces it for display only. Separately, org_stance_priors recomputes ALIGNED, OPPOSED and UNKNOWN per bill for each directional sector pair from label_3_class. It raises CCCAValidationError if a CCCA anchor bill reads OPPOSED for the bank|credit_union pair.
evidence.transfer: Kim's data ends at the 117th Congress (2022). It can nominate historical candidate contested bills and calibrate the alliance-conflict recompute. Current bills depend on the weaker Haiku lane. Registry admission stays an owner ruling. An OPPOSED pair from inferred labels is a lead, not a fact.

evidence.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports
evidence.claim: Positions are measured as interest group x bill. Legislators enter only as context nodes in the GNN graph, through sponsor/cosponsor relations and legislator-lobbyist prior-work relations. The selected configuration is 'Base Graph + legislator-lobbyist'. The paper does not measure a position or contact between a group and a member.
evidence.system_side: build_dyad_signs joins signed org-bill rows to sponsor/cosponsor rosters by canonical bill, counting probability >= 0.7 as support and <= 0.3 as oppose. efficiency_layers z-scores signed_non_cu_opposition_count into signed_non_cu_opposition_z, which is one component of contest_index.
evidence.transfer: Kim's measure stops at the bill. Pushing it onto members through the bill roster brings back the circular sponsor/cosponsor mapping the system already refuted as influence evidence. The dyad counts describe which bills members sponsored, not whom an org targeted. Kim's legislator-lobbyist relation is a revolving-door edge, so influence language is barred on it.

evidence.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports
evidence.claim: Firm size is associated with position type. Comparing firms at the 90th and 10th employment percentiles, larger firms are 19.5 p.p. more likely to lobby and 4.5 p.p. more likely to adopt Monitor. Smaller firms are more likely to Oppose (1.8 p.p.) or Amend (1.3 p.p.). These are associations, not causal effects. Sample: Compustat firm-years 2009-2022, 5,421-7,014 firms per year.
evidence.system_side: classify_client assigns side (credit_union, bank or other) from decisive name rules first. When no name rule fires, it falls back to a NAICS-based classification, and a NAICS conflict with a name match is tagged in the rule string.
evidence.transfer: Kim's sample is Compustat firms and says nothing about trade associations. The claim that the system's 22 pinned fintech/crypto firms hold 56 positions with one directional label was not found and is UNVERIFIED. Treat any reading that associations are the directional filers as a descriptive lead, not a replication.

evidence.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
evidence.claim: Organizations that lobby and organizations that give through PACs barely overlap. Per year, as a share of all politically active organizations: 1998 (n=9,076) 64% lobby only, 24% PAC only, 12% both; 2008 (n=15,729) 70/20/10. Pooled 1998-2018 (Figure 4): 3,427 organizations (6.3%) did both; the 6.3% is printed, and its denominator 54,517 is the sum of the four Figure 4 groups (34,038 only lobby, 9,528 only contribute, 3,427 both, 7,524 not active), so it includes inactive organizations. The authors put the yearly overlap at 10-15% and tell researchers not to conflate lobbying and electioneering.
evidence.system_side: Bridge round 3 (look dated 2026-08-01) is CLOSED and UNCORROBORATED: pooled member-level Spearman rho +0.153 (p=0.015) but four-control partial -0.0002, window 2023-2026, pooled N=213 member x industry x cycle pairs from fintech and crypto, two cycles each (credit_union strata coverage-limited and not entering). Fixed consequence wording: FEC exposure is a target-side money prior only and must not be presented as a lobbying-relationship predictor. The LDA side uses a locked 22-lob_id crosswalk.
evidence.transfer: The paper is about organizations; the bridge is about members (where money exposure and lobbying attention land). Different estimands, and the paper does not explain the zero partial. What carries over is the population point: organizations that lobby without a PAC (64-70% of all politically active organizations per year, about 84-88% of lobbying organizations) leave no organizational FEC trace, so FEC cannot be a general lobbying proxy. Federal organizations, 1998-2018, CRP definitions. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

evidence.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
evidence.claim: Among all politically active organizations, 64-70% per year lobby without making PAC contributions; among lobbying organizations alone that is roughly 84% (1998) to 88% (2008). The share of PAC contribution dollars coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% (1998) to about 30% (2018). Contributions by employees or contract lobbyists are not counted as organizational giving.
evidence.system_side: The 'FEC leads LDA' heuristic number comes from _lead_months, computed as months from the end of the LobbyView finance-joined filing year to the latest FEC transaction date: a data-freshness gap, not an estimated lag. The opposition prior's FEC basis is itemized individual giving by employees and executives of 10 sample companies per industry plus limited corporate rows, not industry-complete.
evidence.transfer: Low overlap undercuts any reading in which one organization's giving foreshadows its own later lobbying, because most lobbying organizations do not give through a PAC. The paper measures organizational/affiliated-PAC money, not the employee giving this prior uses, so it bounds the lead wording rather than refuting it. The freshness reading of lead_months is unaffected. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

evidence.title: Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics
evidence.claim: Lobbying reports need not identify the politicians contacted, so the network is built indirectly: A_ij = number of bills group i lobbied that politician j sponsored (113th Congress, k = 8). The authors call this 'a type of political connection' and read recurring co-occurrence as 'shared involvement on specific political issues', while stating that lobbying a bill 'does not necessarily imply political ties to its sponsor'. They make no claim that the link is contact or that lobbying causes sponsorship. Window: 113th Congress; denominator: lobbied bills with an identified sponsor.
evidence.system_side: build_network_2021_rebuild.py credits every legislator who sponsored OR cosponsored each lobbied bill and emits lob_id x bioguide_id x year x n_bills rows. Project memory records this link as circular: P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so it cannot serve as influence evidence.
evidence.transfer: Same bill-roster construction, but the system's is broader (adds cosponsors) while the paper uses sponsors only, so the dyads are not identical. The paper avoids circularity only because it makes no lobbying-predicts-sponsorship claim; any Melange reuse must stay descriptive. Under D-021 the matrix is an identity source, not an edge or weight source.

evidence.title: Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics
evidence.claim: Table 1 lists the 10 dyads whose observed interactions most exceed biLCM predictions (e.g. Shaheen-NOVO NORDISK 12 observed vs 1.61 estimated; Marino-CVS 10 vs 0.55). The authors suggest explanations from geography, campaign contributions (IHEARTMEDIA with Conaway and Barrasso) and bill-specific stakes, without testing them.
evidence.system_side: The preregistered round-3 FEC x LDA bridge test found money contributes -0.0002 beyond structural controls, so FEC data is excluded as a feature of the lobbying champions residual rank. Project memory records the raw rho as +0.153 and the result as UNCORROBORATED.
evidence.transfer: Suggests testing whether FEC money concentrates on dyads with positive community-model residuals rather than correlating levels. Hypothesis only; anecdotes from one Congress. Residuals on a bill-roster join inherit its circularity for any join outcome; a different control set on the same window is not a successor test.

evidence.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation
evidence.claim: LDA client names were matched to Compustat in four steps: FuzzyWuzzy against 61,478 unique client names; Bureau van Dijk batch search for ISIN and ticker; CRP standardized client names; and a random 5 percent sample of client names checked for publicly traded firms that were missed. The 5 percent sample is a miss (recall) check, not a precision audit. The paper names messy spellings and abbreviations as the main hazard. The matched universe is 67,842 unique lobbying client names (Introduction).
evidence.system_side: classify_client assigns Bank, CU or other. Credit-union names are checked first and are decisive, then trade-association names, then bank names with exclusions. Only when no name rule fires does the function fall back to a NAICS-based side. So NAICS does drive side assignment as a fallback, not only linkage metadata. No random-sample accuracy audit of the classification is recorded.
evidence.transfer: The transferable piece is the 5 percent sample as a recall audit for missed names. The fuzzy matcher is not transferable, and the project's strict-names rule rejects fuzzy acceptance. H&K's firm match leaves out most CUs (not in Compustat, per the analyst; not checked against the paper) and trade-association lobbying such as CUNA and NAFCU, so their match rates and Fact 5 do not carry to CU lobbying.

evidence.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users
evidence.claim: DICN = (1 + CN)(1 + Corr), where Corr is the Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors. At beta = 80% training it has the highest mean AUC (15 random splits) in 8 of 9 networks (e.g. NSC 0.9747 vs CNDP 0.9195; KHN 0.8839 vs SHOPI 0.8509). It loses on UAL (0.9367 vs NCC 0.9416). On test pairs whose nodes share no common neighbour (Exp. 3, compared only with PA, CCPA and SHOPI), it is best in 5 of 9 networks (e.g. KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471).
evidence.system_side: The forecaster scores (bill, member) candidates with ridge logistic regression on prior-Congress HR/S features. The only dyadic feature drawn from the cosponsor graph is the direct prior member-to-sponsor affinity count and rate. The other dyadic terms are attribute-based: same party, state and chamber, NOMINATE distances, and an optional prior committee co-service term. Prior degree and eigenvector centrality are member-level and are computed on an undirected weighted sponsor-cosponsor projection. There is no common-neighbour, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar or second-order similarity feature between sponsor and candidate.
evidence.transfer: The paper uses random edge holdout on nine static benchmark graphs (34-3,772 nodes) that it does not describe as weighted or directed; it lists those as future work. The forecaster is temporal (the Congress t-1 graph predicts Congress t joins) and bill-level. Its prior graph is an undirected weighted projection, and its affinity feature is ordered (member, sponsor). Paper margins over the best baseline run from about 0.007 to 0.055 AUC, with no variance reported. A sponsor-candidate CN or DICN feature on the prior-Congress graph is a cheap candidate to test against the affinity baseline. Exp. 3 concerns pairs with no common neighbour, which is a different subset from pairs with zero direct prior affinity, so it should not be read as evidence about zero-affinity pairs. Any lift is UNVERIFIED until shown on the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).

evidence.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Within-politician first-time-donation designs find donations followed by lobbying on the member's bills. Table 1 pooled coefficients 0.041, 0.048, 0.047, 0.023 (SE 0.006-0.007; N 16,434,912 in table, 16,428,834 in text). Matched DiD Senate 0.075 to 0.110 and House 0.086 to 0.127 over t+0 to t+3 (3,778 Senate and 5,497 House instances). Committee-linked PAC lobbying rises 0.103 to 0.147, versus sponsorship 0.029 to 0.037. Lobbying does not predict later donations, except a small sponsor-lobbying term in App K.
evidence.system_side: Per the analyst: a member-level cross-sectional Spearman-type rank correlation (the code output label says pooled fractional-rank Spearman rho) between member FEC exposure and LobbyView n_bills for 22 lob_ids, with four controls (party, chamber, volume, committee). Raw rho +0.153 and four-control partial -0.0002 were not checked against a results file in this pass. Constants and wording confirmed in fec/lobbying/fec_lda_bridge3_look.py lines 57-80 (CONTROL_NAMES, OVERCONTROL_SENTENCE, UNCORROBORATED wording).
evidence.transfer: Paper design: firm-politician pair fixed effects, year FE, first-time donation timing, 2008-2018 manufacturing firms. Bridge: member-level cross-section, 2023-26, 22 financial-sector clients, committee control. Different estimand, so the paper does not test the bridge. The paper does not say its committee channel is absorbed by a committee control in a cross-section; that overcontrol reading is the analyst inference (and the code's OVERCONTROL_SENTENCE). The paper is observational and says so (pp.3, 29).

evidence.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Outcome is a firm lobbying a bill tied to politician j through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee referral, with bills matched by number and title because LDA reports have no member names or unique bill IDs. Bill-linked reports are 0.25M of 1.27M (about 20%) and cover about 97% of lobbying spending. The authors call the estimates a conservative lower bound.
evidence.system_side: fec/lobbying/lobby_interactions.py lines 4-5 describe the shipped network as (organization, member, year) counts of whether an organization lobbied a bill the member sponsored or cosponsored. The claim P(joined given lobbied) equals 1 by construction is the analyst gloss and is not stated in those lines.
evidence.transfer: The paper uses the same roster join, but its treatment is donation timing, not the join itself, and it treats the outcome as bill involvement, not contact. Neither the paper nor the code supports reading the join as influence or contact (consistent with D-021). The paper's own committee-referral arm is absent from the system's join.

evidence.title: Corporate lobbying, political action committees, and market concentration
evidence.claim: Lobbying (Tables 3-5, annual N = 116,242) and PAC (Tables 6-7, election-year N = 62,198 and 62,558) are estimated in separate regressions on different samples. The paper does not estimate them jointly, and 'never in sequence' is an inference from table structure, not an explicit statement.
evidence.system_side: fec_lda_bridge3_look.py builds a Pearson rho and a partial correlation controlling for party, chamber, volume and committee (CONTROL_NAMES line 57; partial() and result dict around lines 1066-1085). The four-control partial of -0.0002 appears in lobby_forecast.py and lobby_champions.py comments. The raw rho of +0.153 was not located in the cited folder and is not asserted here.
evidence.transfer: The paper gives no evidence on whether PAC giving leads lobbying or how much the two overlap, so it neither revives nor refutes the bridge. The claim that Furnas et al. show the sharper overlap relation comes from the vault, not from this paper.

evidence.title: Lobbying ROI: An Analysis under the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 (also: Measuring Rates of Return for Lobbying Expenditures)
evidence.claim: Five firms lobbied against the AJCA for alternative tax plans and are not counted in the lobbying group (fn 99, p.28). A sensitivity analysis drops five repatriating lobbyists with uncertain support and raises ROI to 228:1 (fn 100, p.30). Coalition lobbyists out-returned solo lobbyists (257 vs 154). The paper does not describe the provision as lacking organized counter-lobbying.
evidence.system_side: fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py is a per-bill standard, advisory or contested registry. Its docstring gives ratification 2026-07-31, contested records supply an explicit per-bill counterparty set, and no consumer reads it yet (CONTESTED_V1 is planned). Verified.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports only a design implication: returns on a provision with little organized opposition may overstate what contested bills would show. The counter-lobbying evidence is five firms on the other side, so the uncontested label should be softened to five firms lobbied against it. The paper never studies contested bills.

evidence.title: Predicting Positive and Negative Links in Online Social Networks
evidence.claim: Using all 16 signed directed triad counts (which include the 4 positive-only path types) instead of only those 4 positive-only path counts raises accuracy for predicting a positive edge on matched non-edge pairs (chance 0.50): 0.5612 to 0.5911 Epinions, 0.5579 to 0.5953 Slashdot, 0.6983 to 0.7114 Wikipedia (gains 1.3 to 3.7 points).
evidence.system_side: cosponsor_forecast.py feature list uses prior cosponsorship history, network degree and eigenvector, NOMINATE, party, state, chamber, seniority, committee terms, bill type and policy area. It has no signed or mention-derived feature. prior_sponsor_affinity is a count of prior-Congress HR/S cosponsorships with the sponsor. METHOD_NOTE confirms a fixed ridge lambda of 1.0.
evidence.transfer: Gains are 1.3 to 3.7 points on a matched-embeddedness task and may vanish against a cosponsorship-history baseline, which the forecaster must beat first. Only references dated before the forecast Congress may enter. The paper's comparison also changes feature count, so the gain is attributable to the added signed types only.

evidence.title: Negative Link Prediction in Social Media
evidence.claim: Accuracy is misleading under extreme imbalance: a trivial all-missing classifier reaches 99.99 percent accuracy (Sec. 5.1 pp. 92-93). Imbalance is 1:4131 and 1:2534 (Sec. 4.1 p. 90). Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting, and NeLP parameters are set per site, with no held-out tuning protocol described (Sec. 5.2 p. 93).
evidence.system_side: Confirmed: precision_at_k uses cutoffs 10, 25 and 50, bill-averaged (lines 1796-1853). split_verdict compares model average precision with the best of named baselines B1 member propensity, B2 sponsor affinity and B3 party match (lines 1865-1869 and 2063-2105). Average precision is the comparison metric, and no accuracy metric appears in cosponsor_forecast.py. Not confirmed: the frozen-before-scoring clause. That file has no freeze or pre-registration language, so the clause is removed here unless another artifact shows it.
evidence.transfer: The metric choice carries across domains. Tang's unspecified tuning protocol and best-setting baseline reporting are a negative example of protocol, not a template for the system.

evidence.title: Cue-Taking in Congress: Interest Group Signals from Dear Colleague Letters
evidence.claim: Bill-level endorsement signals predict cosponsor counts: max endorser standardized eigenvector centrality coef 0.055 (SE 0.011) and endorser count coef 0.007 (SE 0.001), both p<.001, negative binomial with Congress FE, N = 6,597 House bills with supportive Dear Colleague letters, 106th-111th Congresses. Predicted cosponsors: 33 for a bill endorsed only by unconnected groups (score -0.2053) or with no endorsements; 38 with centrality 2.51 (Anti-Defamation League); 51 with centrality 7.66 (Planned Parenthood).
evidence.system_side: cosponsor_forecast.py feature list (lines 117-142) is a ridge-logistic model. It uses member-dyad features (prior sponsor affinity, prior member cosponsorships, network degree and eigenvector, NOMINATE distances, party, state, seniority, prior coservice, member on referred committee) PLUS bill-level and sponsor-level covariates (bill_committee_referrals, bill_type, policy_area, sponsor_majority_party). The analyst claim of member-dyad features only is wrong. No endorsement or outside-support feature exists (confirmed). The 265,396-row count and unscored status were not found in the repo.
evidence.transfer: Paper estimates are pooled across Congresses and both parties with no party or majority strata reported, so quote as UNSTRATIFIED. The outcome is a bill-level cosponsor count, not a dyad join. Any added bill-level signal must be dated before introduction. Endorsements are public pro-bill signals, but the paper does not show they reflect group influence because solicitation direction is unresolved (footnote 11). LDA counts are not a substitute under D-021.

evidence.title: Cue-Taking in Congress: Interest Group Signals from Dear Colleague Letters
evidence.claim: Footnote 11 (p. 170): a member reviewing a Dear Colleague letter cannot distinguish an endorsement the member solicited from one the interest group solicited from a sponsor. P. 171: endorsers listed together on a letter may not have any interaction, and endorsements were likely pulled together by a member's office.
evidence.system_side: bill_lobbying_sidecar.py docstring (lines 10-20) confirmed: LDA filings never name the members lobbied, and the sidecar ships only a bill-level interaction total. The stronger claim that P(joined given lobbied) = 1 by construction, so the link was refuted, was NOT found in the cited code or sidecar.
evidence.transfer: The paper's endorsement channel is observed by members, which is a stronger channel than an LDA bill mention. Its authors leave solicitation direction unresolved, which supports caution about reading bill co-occurrence as influence. The paper does not discuss LDA filings.

evidence.title: Emerging Late Adolescent Friendship Networks and Big Five Personality Traits: A Social Network Approach
evidence.claim: Reciprocity 1.73 (SE .11), transitivity .14 (SE .02) and distance-2 -.52 (SE .06) were all significant. Adding transitivity and distance-2 improved fit in all 10 groups (chi-square 15.68 to 93.43, df 1), so a model of independent pairs misfits network tie formation.
evidence.system_side: The ridge-logistic forecaster uses pair and individual features: prior sponsor affinity, prior member cosponsorships, network degree and eigenvector, NOMINATE distances, same party/state/chamber, committee features. It has no term for reciprocation (has the sponsor previously cosponsored this member's bills?) and none for closure (shared cosponsor partners).
evidence.transfer: Transfer is moderate in method and weak in evidence. Reciprocity and closure in friendship nominations do not establish the same effects in cosponsorship; the component's own question about Brandenberger reciprocity is the legislative test. Here 'reciprocity' means tie reciprocation and must not be confused with the money reciprocity that is still unvalidated (D-104..D-108). Any added feature counts only after the frozen 265,396-prediction forecast is scored against a non-circular outcome, and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

evidence.title: Shadowing and shielding: Effective heuristics for continuous influence maximisation in the voting dynamics
evidence.claim: Against a passive opponent with known allocation w_b, the low-allocation optimum has a term linear in w_bi with common coefficient c = (Ba/Bb - 1): shadow the opponent's targets if Ba > Bb, avoid them if Ba < Bb (Eq 5, low-allocation limit only; a degree term enters only when positivity constraints bind). Continuous shadowing plus shielding is within 1.89e-3 of the numerical optimum under budget advantage (degree 2.09e-2, uniform 2.14e-2). Under disadvantage it is 7.28e-4 vs 2.12e-3 for discrete degree targeting (K=16, 15 instances).
evidence.system_side: contested_bills.py docstring says no consumer exists today for the CONTESTED_V1 dial. The registry is display-only: build_dashboard_bundle.py lines 731-745 loads it and shows it in the posture block with consumer False, fed to no engine. build_opposition_prior.py lines 1528-1542 defines w_b as relational exposure (independent expenditures, communication costs and conduit money removed) summing to 1.0, labelled coalition-builder adversary substrate / shadowing layer. The paper's dynamics are an unnoised voter model on one academic email network, so c and the gap sizes are not calibrated for Congress. The sign of the response needs the per-bill budget ratio measured first. UNVERIFIED for this system until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: LobbyView: Firm-level Lobbying & Congressional Bills Database
evidence.claim: The abstract says LobbyView bridges politicians' sponsorship of bills with reported lobbying by interest groups. Section 2 steps 1-5 describe only matching report text to bill identities (number, Congress, title, range). No step describes a legislator link or any contact. So the member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record. The paper does not describe this join itself.
evidence.transfer: Holds for the system join. The paper's sponsorship wording is only the abstract phrase, and the system's join is wider: sponsor plus all cosponsors. collect_lobbyview.py line 446 records a 2026-08-01 check that BECU 2021 has 181 edges equal to 1 sponsor plus 180 cosponsors of H.R. 1996. That is a code comment; it was not re-run here.

evidence.title: LobbyView: Firm-level Lobbying & Congressional Bills Database
evidence.claim: Filing-year Congress assignment fails. Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577 (Safe Data Act), a 112th Congress bill, not the 113th. LobbyView considers the three preceding Congresses by default, picks the candidate with highest cosine similarity to surrounding text (Eq. 1), falls back to the filing-year Congress if no number matches, and propagates a Congress across the report by majority vote.
evidence.system_side: The 2021+ rebuild binds each formal citation to the filing Congress unless an 'of 20XX' suffix in the same segment resolves to an earlier Congress (_resolve_mention_congress; current mentions set the resolved Congress to filing_congress). The rebuild has no cosine-similarity lookback and no report-level propagation. A search for cosine, propagate, majority and argmax returned no hits.
evidence.transfer: Paper side reproduced. Under the rebuild rule, the paper's own example would bind to the 113th Congress. Risk concentrates in filings made early in a new Congress (odd-year first sessions). The paper gives no rate, so the size of the error in the rebuild is UNVERIFIED.

evidence.title: Bulk Ingestion of Congressional Actions and Materials Dataset (BICAM)
evidence.claim: Bill numbers and titles extracted from LD-2 Section 16 are matched by distance measures to the Bills component (421,764 bills, 6th-119th Congress); low-confidence matches get extra scrutiny. The linkage is said to detect significantly more bill lobbying than Kim and Kunisky 2021 and to capture ex-post lobbying. The main text gives no match count, precision, recall or threshold.

Generous outputs keep ambiguous-title fan-out; strict outputs need a same-segment formal citation. Slash-joined citations parse only the left side (line 19; 2 of 376 distinct bills, 0.5 percent, 2023-24 association corpus). LD-2 has no member or position field (lobby_interactions.py line 18).
evidence.transfer: BICAM fits only as a candidate second path for bill-mention resolution. A bill-to-sponsor join from it is a roster edge with P(credited given lobbied) = 1 by construction and adds no contact signal. Precision and recall sit in the Supplementary Information, which this check did not have.

evidence.title: Bulk Ingestion of Congressional Actions and Materials Dataset (BICAM)
evidence.claim: BICAM supplies Bill-LDA linkages, not the LDA filings, and points to LobbyView and OpenSecrets as the compilations of LDA data. Members are keyed by bioguide_id and icpsr. evidence.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying

evidence.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
evidence.claim: Kang (2012) builds an all-pay contest model of counteractive lobbying, estimated on energy groups' support and opposition for policies in 110th Congress bills, and finds the expenditure effect on enactment is very small. Baumgartner et al. (98 issues) find both sides mobilize roughly equal resources and policy is usually stable.
evidence.system_side: contested_bills.py docstring: per-bill registry ratified by Paul 2026-07-31; contested records supply a per-bill explicit counterparty set; standard mode is the default; advisory records are display-only; CONTESTED_V1 is a future dial and no consumer exists today.
evidence.transfer: An all-pay contest needs bill-level spending by both sides. LDA issue codes and bill mentions may supply that at the bill level, not the member level. The equal-mobilization finding warns that relative spend may predict little. Admission must stay with Paul's ratification.

evidence.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
evidence.claim: Money is not transferred explicitly to politicians as campaign contributions are, so lobbying is a distinct channel (p.4). Lobbying expenditures are about five times interest-group campaign contributions (pp.5-6). The essay does not address whether campaign giving leads lobbying.
evidence.system_side: Bridge round-3 look: raw rho +0.153 member-blocked p=.0146, but four-control partial -0.0002, tier UNCORROBORATED. The 42-month FEC lead is recorded as intact in the collector note and is a candidate heuristic only.
evidence.transfer: The paper gives no evidence that giving leads lobbying. A lead test would need an exogenous-shock design rather than more controls.

evidence.title: Spillovers from regulating corporate campaign contributions
evidence.claim: Firm-cycles at the PAC limit associate with +549,166 dollars of LDA lobbying (firm FE and Fama-French 49 industry-by-cycle FE; 2000-2008; 787 firms; 2,783 firm-cycles). The at-limit by post-BCRA interaction is +539,008 (Table 6; 787 firms). LDA filings do not name candidates, so firm-candidate lobbying cannot be linked.
evidence.system_side: Bridge round 3 tested member-level FEC exposure against LDA attention (2023-2026; credit_union, fintech, crypto). Raw rho +0.1525, four-control partial -0.0002, tier UNCORROBORATED, per the results block of the prereg. FEC framed as a target-side money prior only.
evidence.transfer: The unit is the firm, not the member, so the paper neither revives nor contradicts the member-level null. A transferable design would test an organization's giving at the cap against that organization's own LDA spend, with time fixed effects; that design is the analyst's suggestion, not the paper's.

evidence.title: Spillovers from regulating corporate campaign contributions
evidence.claim: LDA disclosures do not identify the candidates or members lobbied. The authors relate only firm-level lobbying totals to PAC behaviour and approximate the mapping with a stepwise function.
evidence.system_side: The lobby interactions ledger links an organization to a member when it lobbied a bill that member sponsored or cosponsored (docstring lines 4-6). The paper does not say whether P(joined given lobbied) is 1 by construction; the REFUTED-as-influence verdict comes from the analyst and the brain, not this code or the paper.
evidence.transfer: Confirms only that LDA rows do not name members, a measurement fact. The paper offers no contact measure to reuse.

evidence.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
evidence.claim: LDA filings do not require an amount per specific topic (p.19). Issue intensity is proxied by the number of years a topic is listed and by keyword matches in specific-issue text (H-1B, L-1, PERM, high-skill bills), pp.5-6.
evidence.system_side: contested_bills.py allowed record keys are bill, congress, mode, counterparty_industries, active_from, active_to, ratified_by, ratified_date and note; there is no spend field. Engine wiring and the bank-vs-CU spend question were not checked.
evidence.transfer: A relative-spend test per bill needs report dollars apportioned across issues and bills, which Kerr avoids; a filing or issue-mention count is the defensible proxy. LDA stays an identity and measurement source, never an edge or weight (D-021).
